Introduction:
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) continues to be a deadly infection. In 2022, there were an estimated 630 000 (480 000–880 000) deaths worldwide and 1.3 million new infections globally, of which more than half occurred in Eastern and Southern Africa (ESA) [ 1 ]. Combination antiretroviral treatment (ART) suppresses HIV viraemia and is highly effective in reducing HIV-associated mortality [ 2–4 ] and preventing onward HIV transmission [ 5 , 6 ]. Consequently, treatment has been adopted as a public health strategy to prevent new HIV infections (treatment-as-prevention, TasP) [ 1 , 7 , 8 ]. Progress in implementing TasP programs is primarily measured through the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) ‘95–95–95’ targets, with the aim that 95% of people living with HIV (PLHIV) are aware of their status, 95% of those aware are on antiretroviral therapy, and 95% of those on ART achieve viral suppression. All countries in ESA committed to attaining these targets by 2025 [ 9 ] as part of achieving UN Sustainable Development Goals [ 10 , 11 ].

By January 2025, and prior to sudden cuts in global aid funding by the US government [ 12 ], many countries in ESA either attained or had been close to attaining 95–95–95 targets at a population level [ 13 , 14 ]. Maintaining HIV epidemic decline remains a central public health priority across ESA countries and novel methods to measure HIV epidemic control could help to direct future prevention efforts more efficiently. One such approach focuses on stratifying 95–95–95 targets by age and gender, which highlights inequalities in treatment coverage [ 19 ]. However, these metrics do not quantify how HIV viraemia is distributed across populations or in which populations viraemia is concentrated, and may not be predictive of incidence declines [ 15–18 ]. Consequently, they may not provide a complete understanding of the people most at risk of HIV-related mortality and onward transmission, which is necessary to tailor effective prevention interventions.

In this study, we consider a complementary metric for assessing HIV control: the ‘profile’ of how infection burden and HIV viraemia are distributed across age- and gender-specific population subgroups. We compute infection and viraemia profiles and compare the implied priority populations for targeted prevention to those obtained from evaluating 95–95–95 targets on population-based, longitudinal data from the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS)—a large population-based HIV surveillance cohort in southern Uganda. Our analyses were conducted across two distinct settings: in agrarian villages and semi-urban trading centres with population pyramids typical of most ESA communities and in Lake Victoria fishing communities with atypical population structures and very high HIV prevalence. The study time frame of 2013–19 coincided with the national expansion of ART programs.
Methods:
### Study population

The RCCS is a population-based cohort of individuals aged 15–49 years in communities in and around Rakai District [ 20 ] that was established in 1994 by the Rakai Health Sciences Program (RHSP). Between July 2013 and May 2019, four survey rounds [ 16–19 ] were conducted in four Lake Victoria fishing and 36 inland agrarian and semi-urban communities [ 21 ]. In brief, at each survey round, the RCCS conducted a household census and subsequently invited all individuals aged 15–49 years and residing in the communities with intention to stay for ≥1 month to participate. Consent was obtained privately by a trained interviewer. Following consent, participants were interviewed in a private location—typically a tent—for demographic characteristics as well as behavioural and healthcare behaviour, and asked to provide a blood sample for HIV testing and future laboratory studies. All participants were offered free tests, pretest and post-test counselling, and referrals to ART services if living with HIV.

### Population sizes

Age- and gender-specific population sizes in each survey round were estimated from line-list data of census-eligible individuals reported by household heads during the census. Reported ages tended to reflect grouping patterns around multiples of five, which we disaggregated by smoothing population sizes over age [ 22 ] ( Supplementary Text ).

### Measurement of HIV serostatus and viraemia

Testing was performed through a combination of three rapid tests with confirmation of positive, faintly positive, and discordant results by at least two Enzyme Immunoasays (EIAs) and Western blot or DNA PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) [ 23 ]. Overall, 99.7% of participants accepted HIV testing across survey rounds. Among participants with HIV, HIV-1 viral load was measured on stored serum samples by using the Abbott real-time m2000 assay (Abbott Laboratories, IL, USA). Viral loads were obtained from 99.4% of participants with HIV [ 24–26 ]. Viral suppression was defined as a viral load of <1000 HIV RNA copies/ml plasma, following the recommendations of the World Health Organization [ 27 ] at the time. People who did not achieve viral suppression were defined as viraemic. We estimated population-level HIV seroprevalence (i.e. probability for an individual to have HIV) with a non-parametric Bayesian model over the age of individuals stratified by gender, survey round, and community type (i.e. fishing vs. inland) by using the data from first-time participants as a proxy for non-participating individuals [ 22 ] ( Supplementary Text and Supplementary Fig. S1 ). We used the same model to estimate the proportion of individuals exhibiting viraemia among people with HIV and among all individuals ( Supplementary Text ).

Results:
### Age and gender burden profiles of HIV infection

From July 2013 to May 2019, 37 743 individuals participated at least once across four RCCS survey rounds ( Fig. 1 ). Of these, 22 215 (58.86%) participated for the first time ( Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Inland communities had expansive population pyramids with a predominantly young population, consistently with the rapid population growth across Uganda and ESA [ 28 ]. In contrast, fishing communities had constrictive population pyramids comprising primarily working-age adults (20–40 years) and substantially fewer children or women than in inland communities ( Table 1 and Fig. 2b ).

To describe the burden of HIV infection, we initially followed the typical approach to reporting HIV seroprevalence and estimated the proportion of individuals in each 1-year age band who had HIV, i.e. positive HIV serostatus within age bands ( Fig. 2c , and Supplementary Fig. S3 ). The distinct population pyramids of these communities also prompted us to characterize the infection profile ( Fig. 2c , black). The infection profile centred more strongly on younger populations than the statistics of HIV seroprevalence within each 1-year age band might suggest. For example, by 2019, in inland communities, half of the women with HIV were 28–40 years old and half of the men with HIV were 31–42 years old ( Table 2 ). We also found substantial differences in infection burden by gender. In inland communities, women contributed 66.2% (63.8%–68.4%) to HIV infections, as the higher seroprevalence of women might suggest, but, in fishing communities, women contributed only 55.2% (53.1%–57.3%) due to gender imbalance in the population structures, contrary to what the higher seroprevalence in women compared with that in men might suggest ( Table 1 ).

### Progress towards 95–95–95 targets

We next characterized progress towards 95–95–95 targets in the fishing communities in which TasP has been prioritized since 2013 and in the inland communities in which Universal Test and Treat was implemented in late 2016. We performed 13 844 viral load measurements in 6677 of 6705 (99.6%) participants with HIV. Notably, the proportion of people with HIV exhibiting viraemia decreased from 40.6% (38.4%–42.8%) in 2013 to 17.6% (15.8%–19.6%) in 2019 in inland communities and from 53.5% (51.1%–56.0%) in 2013 to 14.4% (12.4%–16.7%) in 2019 in fishing communities. Gender-specific trends are reported in Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. S4 .

### Trends in population-level viraemia

Considering viraemia at a population level, the proportion of individuals with unsuppressed viraemia decreased from 4.9% (4.6%–5.3%) in 2013 to 1.9% (1.7%–2.2%) in 2019 in inland communities and from 19.1% (18.0%–20.4%) in 2013 to 4.7% (4.0%–5.5%) in 2019 in fishing communities, with gender-specific results reported in Table 2 . Thus, while suppression levels among PLHIV were higher in fishing communities compared with inland communities, suppression levels in the population were lower in fishing communities rather than inland communities due to a higher HIV prevalence in fishing communities.

### Age and gender profiles of HIV viraemia

To characterize the age- and gender-specific populations in whom viraemia was concentrated, we first considered the proportion of age- and gender-stratified PLHIV who had unsuppressed HIV. By 2019, in inland communities, the proportion of PLHIV exhibiting viraemia was highest in men aged 23–27 years [49.8% (39.9%–60.3%)] and in fishing communities in men aged 28–32 years [28.2% (20.0%–41.2%)] ( Fig. 3 ). Among women, this proportion was the highest in women aged 15–17 years in inland communities [30.3% (18.7%–44.0%)] and in women aged 18–22 years in fishing communities [23.9% (16.2%–34.0%)]. The proportion of PLHIV exhibiting viraemia was larger in first-time participants ( Supplementary Figures S4 and S5 ).

Then, we characterized the population subgroups in which viraemia was concentrated. Figure 4a compares the proportion of women and men with HIV in each age band who had unsuppressed viraemia to the viraemia profiles. Viraemia was not centred in the age groups furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets. In inland communities, women aged 15–19 years were the furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets in 2019, but we estimate that they contributed only 4.9% (3.0%–7.3%) to people with unsuppressed viraemia. Instead, women aged 20–24 and 25–29 years each contributed ∼10% to people with viraemia in 2019, although these age groups were either close to or had already exceeded the 95–95–95 targets. Similarly, in inland communities, men aged 20–24 years were furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets in 2019, but we estimate that they contributed only 5.4% (3.9%–7.4%) to the unsuppressed viraemia. Rather, men aged 25–29 and 30–34 years each contributed ∼10% to viraemia in 2019. Similar patterns were observed in fishing communities ( Fig. 4a ).

Figure 4b depicts temporal changes in absolute suppression levels, as well as shifts in the viraemia profile. Even though we found a steady increase in the median age of PLHIV in both genders and locations, the age profile of people exhibiting viraemia remained relatively stable over time ( Supplementary Table S2 ).
Discussion:
This study documents remarkable achievements in reducing unsuppressed HIV viraemia in southern Uganda in 2013–19 and identifies the age- and gender-specific populations in whom unsuppressed viraemia is concentrated by using population-based surveillance data from the RCCS in Uganda. Following expanding TasP programs, fishing communities witnessed faster increases in suppression levels among PLHIV than inland communities, with overall levels surpassing the 95–95–95 targets by 2019. Yet, HIV incidence remained higher in fishing communities despite additional interventions such as Pre Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) [ 29 ]. This may be explained by our finding that the burden of unsuppressed viraemia in the population remained ∼2.5 times larger in fishing communities, reflecting a higher HIV prevalence, and suggests that reaching 95–95–95 metrics may be insufficient to lower the incidence to below the elimination thresholds [ 30 ], especially in countries with elevated HIV burdens [ 31 ]. Furthermore, current UNAIDS targets recommend that the 95–95–95 targets are met within subpopulations stratified by age and gender [ 32 ], thereby supporting the prioritization of interventions to those subgroups that are the furthest from achieving the targets and improving barriers and inequalities in treatment coverage [ 19 ]. However, these subgroups may not predominantly contribute to unsuppressed viraemia in the population. For example, we found that most individuals exhibiting unsuppressed viraemia were men in both inland and fishing communities, although fewer men had HIV than women. In addition, the age groups that contributed the most to unsuppressed viraemia in the population were not those that were furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets. In RCCS inland communities, young individuals aged 15–24 years constituted approximately two-fifths of the census-eligible population, but only one-fifth of the population exhibiting viraemia. In fact, the lower suppression levels commonly reported among young PLHIV [ 13 , 33–40 ] are counterbalanced by the small absolute number of young PLHIV. This observation is typically missing from studies supporting the prioritization of younger age groups in ESA based on 95–95–95 targets [ 45 ]. The viraemia profiles that we estimate provide evidence for reaching and treating a wide subset of the population—men aged 25–34 years and women aged 20–39 years, who predominantly contribute to unsuppressed viraemia in the population.

While we assessed age- and gender-specific profiles of both HIV infection and viraemia in this study, the latter metric provides a cross-sectional description of individuals most at risk of HIV mortality and onward transmission. Hence, we propose the viraemia profile as a new metric for HIV control. We observed that the viraemia profiles revealed similar relative contributions of men and women, and larger relative contributions of middle-aged individuals [ 25–34 ] than younger individuals [ 15–24 ], whereas these important observations were obscured in age- and gender-stratified 95–95–95 targets. Furthermore, unlike the 95–95–95 targets [ 15 , 16 ], the population burden of HIV viraemia has been shown to be strongly predictive of population HIV incidence [ 18 , 41 ].

The findings of this study need to be considered in the context of several limitations. First, following the survey protocol in place during the study period, our study population was limited to individuals aged 15–49 years. Accordingly, we are not able to quantify HIV prevalence among individuals aged ≥50 years or viral suppression outcomes in children (<15 years old) with HIV. Thus, the reported age- and gender-specific percentages in the burden profiles in the population aged 15–49 years should not be interpreted as fractions of the entire population. Second, this study only considered RCCS data. However, the demographic and epidemiological patterns seen in Rakai are typical of rural and semi-urban populations across ESA, including expansive population pyramids [ 28 ], age and gender trends in HIV prevalence [ 42 ], and gender gaps in suppression levels [ 13 , 33–40 ]. It seems likely that individuals aged 25–34 years may be predominantly contributing to HIV viraemia across the subcontinent. Third, to generalize our results from study participants to the population, we assumed that first-time study participants were representative of non-participants by age- and gender-specific prevalence and viral suppression levels. If viral suppression among non-participants is lower than among first-time participants, then the reported viral suppression levels could be overestimates. Fourth, considering HIV prevention, the age profiles in onward HIV transmission correspond only approximately to those of viraemia and, in particular, men tend to contribute more to heterosexual transmission than viraemia may suggest [ 22 , 43 , 44 ]. Additionally, transmission risk factors such as sexual behaviour are highly heterogeneous across individuals of the same age and gender [ 45–47 ]. This supports complementing population-based metrics such as the viraemia profiles with individual-level metrics, e.g. HIV acquisition risk scores [ 48 , 49 ], to further guide the next generation of targeted prevention policies.

As of December 2024, the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) program had supported >20 million PLHIV with lifesaving treatment corresponding to approximately two-thirds of all PLHIV accessing ART globally [ 50 ] and has over the past two decades saved >26 million lives through HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support programs, and averted almost 5 million HIV infections in children [ 12 ]. In early 2025, the USA abruptly cut PEPFAR funding, causing service disruptions, HIV clinic closures, and fear among people who depend on wide-ranging PEPFAR-supported services [ 51 ]. It is now critical to monitor and mitigate the impacts of these unprecedented funding cuts on people affected by HIV. This must include population-based surveillance of HIV incidence and viral suppression as key determinants of prospective morbidity, mortality, and transmission risk, to guide the global HIV response through a looming, man-made global health emergency. Future surveillance efforts should include population-level measures of HIV viraemia to help direct HIV control and elimination efforts more effectively.
